name: Eastern Kadazan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hurlbut, Hope M. 1988. Verb morphology in Eastern Kadazan. Pacific Linguistics B-97. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, Research School of Pacific Studies, Australian National University. viii+151 pp. DOI 10.15144/PL-B97 (online edition 2015, CC BY-SA 4.0, sealang.net/CRCL).
catalog_locator: Appendix 1, 'Orthography and pronunciation', p. 120, second paragraph; read
catalog_quote: Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word. When suffixes and clitics are added to a stem the stress shifts from the penultimate syllable of the stem to the penultimate syllable of the new word. For example, with the root ongoi the stress is on o giving o'ngoi. With the addition of the suffix -on the stress shifts giving ongoi'on. With the addition of the clitic -ku the stress shifts again giving ongoion'ku.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (phonological) word, counted after all suffixes and enclitics are attached; adding a suffix or an enclitic such as -ku moves the stress one syllable to the right so that it remains penultimate (o'ngoi > ongoi'on > ongoion'ku).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The same appendix notes that sequences of like vowels are interpreted as long vowels (also across affix boundaries) and that glottal stop is marginal; no interaction with stress is described.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, explicitly including suffixed and encliticised forms (the possessive/genitive clitic -ku counts for stress placement), so the domain is the word plus enclitics. Stated as a brief pronunciation note in an orthography appendix of a morphology monograph, not in a full phonological description; no instrumental evidence. Stress-mark spacing in the examples follows the PDF text (the printed forms are o'ngoi, ongoi'on, ongoion'ku with the tick before the stressed syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Hurlbut 1988 (p. 1) describes 'Eastern Kadazan' as spoken along the Labuk River from its mouth to beyond Wonod (96 miles inland from Sandakan), with smaller Mangkaak and Sukang groups on northern tributaries of the Kinabatangan; the data are from the Labuk River variety, i.e. Glottolog dialect Labuk (Kadazan) [labu1250] within Labuk-Kinabatangan Kadazan [labu1249]. The scan's named source 'Hurlbut 1993, Labuk-Kinabatangan Kadazan phonemics' is a different (later, fuller) work that remains unopened.

sources.note: Appendix 1 'Orthography and pronunciation', p. 120 (p. 128): stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; shifts rightward when suffixes and clitics are added so that it stays penultimate in the new word (ongoi > o'ngoi, ongoi'on, ongoion'ku). Nothing on secondary stress. Body of the book is verb morphology; this appendix is the only phonology.
